title: Arrays and strings: where the bugs live
objective: By the end of this lesson you can work with arrays and C strings correctly, and you can explain why the classic string functions are dangerous and what to use instead.

blocks.text: C has no string type. A string is an array of characters with a zero byte marking the end, and an array is a block of memory with no length attached. Every problem in this lesson comes from those two facts.

blocks.caption: Arrays: fixed size, no bounds checking
lines: int scores[5];                    /* uninitialised — contains whatever was there */
int zeroed[5] = {0};              /* every element set to 0 */
scores[0] = 10;
scores[5] = 99;                   /* past the end: compiles, may corrupt something */
size_t n = sizeof ready / sizeof ready[0];   /* 5 — the only way to get the count */

blocks.title: That sizeof trick stops working the moment the array is passed to a function
blocks.text: When you pass an array to a function it becomes a pointer, and sizeof then measures the pointer, not the array — usually 8. This is why every C function that takes an array also takes a length. If a function signature has an array without a length beside it, that is a defect waiting to happen.
Strings are arrays that end in a zero byte

blocks.caption: The terminator is the string
lines: char greeting[] = "hi";      /* 3 bytes: 'h', 'i', '\0' */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof greeting);   /* 3 — includes the terminator */
printf("%zu\n", strlen(greeting));  /* 2 — counts up to the terminator */
char *literal = "hello";     /* points into read-only memory */
literal[0] = 'H';            /* undefined behaviour — usually a crash */
char editable[] = "hello";   /* a copy on the stack — this one you may modify */
editable[0] = 'H';           /* fine */

blocks.title: Lose the terminator and every string function runs off the end
blocks.text: strlen, printf("%s"), strcpy and the rest all keep going until they find a zero byte. If it is missing, they read past the end of your buffer into whatever follows — printing memory that was never yours, or crashing. A great many string bugs are really terminator bugs.
The dangerous functions and their replacements

rows: No size limit at all — removed from the language
Writes until the terminator, however long that is
Same problem, plus it starts at the existing end

blocks.caption: The overflow, in four lines
lines: char small[8];
const char *input = "this is far longer than eight bytes";
strcpy(small, input);        /* writes ~35 bytes into 8 — everything after is corrupted */
snprintf(small, sizeof small, "%s", input);   /* writes 7 bytes plus a terminator */

blocks.title: strncpy is not the safe version of strcpy
blocks.text: It copies at most n bytes — but if the source is n bytes or longer it does not add a terminator, leaving you with a string that no longer ends. It also pads with zeros when the source is shorter, which is slow for large buffers. It was designed for a fixed-width record format, not for safe copying. Prefer snprintf, which always terminates.

blocks.caption: Always pass the length
lines: int sum(const int *values, size_t count) {   /* count is not optional */
int total = 0;
for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) total += values[i];
return total;
printf("%d\n", sum(data, sizeof data / sizeof data[0]));
/* Inside sum, sizeof values is the size of a pointer — the count must come from outside. */

blocks.caption: Rows are laid out one after another
lines: int grid[3][4];              /* 12 ints, contiguous in memory */
/* grid[1][2] is at offset 1*4 + 2 = 6 */
void print_grid(int rows, int cols, int g[rows][cols]) {   /* dimensions come first */
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
printf("%d ", g[r][c]);

blocks.title: Overflow a buffer, then fix it
steps: Write: char small[8]; strcpy(small, "far too long for eight"); printf("%s\n", small);
Run: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O0 -g str.c -o str && ./str      (it may appear to work)
Read the report: buffer name, size, and how far past the end it wrote
Replace strcpy with snprintf(small, sizeof small, "%s", input) and run again
Now print sizeof and strlen of a string and explain the difference to yourself
Write sum(const int *, size_t) and confirm that sizeof inside it gives 8, not the array size
blocks.expected: An overflow that the plain build hides and the sanitizer names exactly, a bounded copy that truncates safely instead, and first-hand proof that an array loses its size the moment it is passed to a function.

cheatsheet: An array is memory with no length attached; there is no bounds checking
sizeof arr / sizeof arr[0] gives the count — but only where the array was declared
Passing an array to a function turns it into a pointer, so always pass the length too
A C string is characters plus a terminating zero byte
sizeof includes the terminator; strlen does not
String literals are read-only; char s[] = "..." makes a modifiable copy
Never gets, strcpy, strcat, or sprintf
Use fgets and snprintf — both take a size and always terminate
strncpy may leave the result unterminated; it is not the safe strcpy
2D arrays are one contiguous block, laid out row after row

checkpoint.prompt: Why must a C function that receives an array also receive its length?

choices.C: Because the array becomes a pointer
choices.D: Because arrays cannot be passed at all

checkpoint.explanation: The array becomes a pointer when passed, so sizeof inside the function measures the pointer, not the array. The size information is lost at the call. A signature with an array and no length is a bug waiting for the wrong input.

checkpoint.prompt: char s[] = "hi"; What are sizeof s and strlen(s)?
checkpoint.explanation: The terminating zero byte is part of the storage (so sizeof counts it) but not part of the length (strlen counts up to it). Mixing the two up is a common source of off-by-one errors.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is strncpy not simply the safe version of strcpy?

choices.A: It was removed from the C standard years ago
choices.C: It may leave the result unterminated
choices.D: It cannot be used with arrays

checkpoint.explanation: If the source is as long as or longer than n, it does not write a terminator — leaving a string that never ends. It was designed for fixed-width records, not for safe copying. snprintf always terminates, which is why it is the recommendation.

checkpoint.prompt: What happens if a character array loses its terminating zero byte?

choices.A: String functions keep reading past the end of the buffer
choices.B: Nothing — the length is stored separately next to the buffer

checkpoint.explanation: The terminator is the only thing that marks the end. Without it, every string function runs off into unrelated memory that was never part of your data, printing or copying whatever is there.

checkpoint.prompt: Why must a function receive an array length?

choices.A: A pointer records the number of elements it references
choices.B: The compiler recovers the length from the first element
choices.C: The parameter is a pointer and carries no array length
choices.D: Array length is always available through sizeof in the callee

checkpoint.explanation: Array length is lost at the call, so the caller must pass it explicitly.

choices.A: Bytes before the terminating NUL byte
choices.B: Characters including the terminating NUL byte
choices.D: Allocated bytes in the pointer target

checkpoint.explanation: strlen counts bytes before the terminating NUL byte, unlike sizeof on the declared array.

checkpoint.prompt: What does sizeof include for char s[] = "hi"?

choices.B: Bytes in a pointer parameter regardless of its declaration

checkpoint.explanation: The array stores h, i, and the terminating zero byte.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a string literal not a writable buffer?

choices.A: It is placed on the stack and can be resized
choices.C: The compiler creates a writable copy for each call
choices.D: Only its length field can change

checkpoint.explanation: Use a character array when code needs a modifiable copy.

checkpoint.prompt: What should fgets receive for a character array?

choices.A: The number of characters already read
choices.C: The address of the next newline

checkpoint.explanation: The size bounds input so the function knows how much storage is available.

checkpoint.prompt: Why use snprintf for formatted text?

choices.B: It treats the format as compile-time checked
choices.C: It writes every formatted character regardless of space
choices.D: It is given the destination capacity

checkpoint.explanation: The capacity lets it limit output and keep a terminating byte when size is nonzero.

choices.A: It has no destination capacity argument
choices.B: It stops after the first whitespace
choices.C: It checks destination capacity before copying

checkpoint.explanation: A long source can write beyond the destination buffer.

checkpoint.prompt: When can strncpy leave no C string?

choices.A: Whenever the destination is larger than the count
choices.B: When the destination was zero-filled first
choices.C: When the source length reaches the count
choices.D: Only when the source contains a newline

checkpoint.explanation: It may copy n bytes without adding a terminating zero byte.

checkpoint.prompt: How are ordinary C two-dimensional arrays stored?

choices.A: Each row as a separately allocated pointer
choices.C: Only nonzero cells in sparse storage

checkpoint.explanation: Rows follow one another in memory, which determines indexing and traversal.

checkpoint.prompt: What must an index satisfy for an array of length n?

choices.A: It may equal n as the final element
choices.C: It must be less than n and nonnegative
choices.D: It must be positive and a multiple of n

checkpoint.explanation: Valid elements run from zero through n minus one.

checkpoint.prompt: What should accompany a pointer used as text?

choices.B: A clear capacity and termination rule

checkpoint.explanation: Callers and callees need the same rule for where writing must stop.
